title: Pipeline Overview
text: Pipeline Overview What this repository builds This repository runs a question-granular, citation-backed answering pipeline that turns a registry of research questions into a reviewed reference site, and it does so twice: once for a Spark Tuning Reference and once for the pipeline's own architecture[1]. Selection between the two happens via --corpus {spark,meta} on every pipeline script, defaulting to spark. scripts/corpus.py holds a Corpus dataclass with SPARK/META profiles, and every path a script touches (registry, per-question answers dir, section-projection dir, content-state sidecar, content manifest, references dir, Chroma path/collection, embedding model, build output, site title) comes from the selected profile rather than a hardcoded constant[1:1]. The spark corpus is the Spark Tuning Reference itself, built over references/ and indexed with the asymmetric question→passage retriever multi-qa-mpnet-base-dot-v1; its build output is index.html[1:2]. The meta corpus is this project's own architecture doc (docs/architecture.md, docs/runbook.md, docs/rules/*.md, AGENTS.md, and the agent/skill files that make up the pipeline). It is indexed via symlinks under references-meta/ with the general symmetric model all-mpnet-base-v2 into a separate Chroma collection, and its build output is meta.html[1:3]. The two corpora never share a registry, a Chroma collection, or a content manifest; each is an independent instance of the same pipeline shape[1:4]. Within either corpus, the atomic unit of the pipeline is the question, not the section: the registry (research/questions.yaml, or its meta counterpart) is the single source of truth holding sections and questions, and every other artifact is a derived projection, never edited directly as a source of truth[1:5]. Content flows one way through the pipeline: registry → per-question answer files (prose plus footnotes and their own ## Sources) → section projections (an ordered concatenation of a section's question answers, with sources merged and deduped) → content pages (brief-driven on first generation, human-owned after that) → the built site, and a downstream artifact is never treated as a source of truth for an upstream one[1:6]. The project's own AGENTS.md restates the operator-facing consequence: every content page is real cited prose, not a placeholder, and new or changed content still flows registry → answer → projection → page[2]. The build output is produced regardless of whether every content page is current. A committed hash sidecar tracks each content page against the sha256 of the section projection it was last generated or accepted from, classifying pages as ungenerated, stale, or ok; the build script checks this before rendering and prints a non-fatal warning banner listing any stale or ungenerated pages, but the build still produces index.html either way[1:7]. Recompute never triggers regeneration on its own; it only flags a page stale, since content pages are human-owned once generated[1:8]. On the Spark side, the resulting pages carry a further constraint tied to why the site exists: its manifest-level anchor IDs are a frozen cross-repo Integration Contract with the sibling sparkforensics repo, so renaming or removing one is a breaking change, and content assembly must read anchors from content/manifest.yaml rather than deriving them from a filename or heading[3]. That contract applies only to the Spark corpus; content/meta/manifest.yaml and meta.html carry no such contract, and their anchors may change freely[3:1]. docs/anchor-map.md reconciles the two, mapping each research answer file to its content file and frozen anchor[4]. The one-way derive chain The chain runs in one direction, front to back: research/questions.yaml → research/answers/q/<id>.md → research/answers/<section-id>.md → content/*.md (and content/bottlenecks/*.md) → index.html[1:9]. Each stage has a role. questions.yaml is the registry of sections and questions with their statuses. Each per-question answer file holds that question's prose plus its own [^id] footnotes and ## Sources block. The section file is a projection: an ordered concatenation of a section's question answers, with ## Sources merged and deduped, and it is the same path the content manifest's assembled_from: already points at. Content pages are brief-driven and only first-generated from that projection, after which they become human-owned. The build turns the content pages into index.html[1:10]. The architecture forbids treating any downstream artifact as a source of truth because research/questions.yaml is the single source of truth for the whole pipeline. Every other artifact (per-question answers, section projections, content pages) is a derived projection, regenerable from the registry and the per-question answer files, never edited as a source of truth itself[1:11]. The registry rules state this directly: never edit a downstream artifact as if it were the source of truth, since per-question answers, section projections, and content pages are all derived projections regenerable from the registry, and recompute always starts at questions.yaml and flows forward[5]. The derive-direction diagram states the same principle as an invariant: every arrow is one-way, and a downstream artifact (a section projection, a content page, the built site) is never a source of truth for an upstream one[1:12]. The project's own AGENTS.md restates the practical consequence for operators: new or changed content still flows registry → answer → projection → page, and questions.yaml remains the authoritative question registry rather than any prose plan or derived array[2:1]. Why the question, not the section, is the atomic unit docs/architecture.md states the design directly: the atomic unit of the answering pipeline is the question, not the section. It goes on to name research/questions.yaml as the single source of truth, holding sections (id, num, title, default_k) as a grouping label and questions (id, section, text, version, k, status) as the working records. Every other artifact, from per-question answer files up through section projections and content pages, is a derived projection regenerable from the registry and those answer files, never a source of truth itself[1:13]. That per-question state (its own version, k, status) is what makes independent recompute possible. add_question.py mints an id and appends a single pending record without mutating any existing record, and recompute_question.py flips exactly one record back to pending and backs up only that question's old answer file, touching no other record or file[5:1]. If the section were the atomic unit, recomputing one question's answer would force treating the whole section's state as dirty; scoping status and versioning to the question lets one question be re-answered, re-versioned, or given its own k without disturbing its siblings. The rest of the pipeline is built around that same grain: the Draft/Verify/Redraft agents are each scoped to a single question, and the answer-question skill runs one question end to end: Draft → Verify → [Redraft → re-Verify] → Humanize → check_prose → project_section → content_state ... → commit[1:14]. The meta corpus's own answer-meta-question skill mirrors this: its input is one question id, and it dispatches the Draft/Verify agents with a one-item question list equal to the record's text[6]. Only after a question is answered does project_section roll it into the section file, by concatenating that section's question answers in registry order and merging their ## Sources blocks[1:15]. The section projection is assembled from finished question-level work, not answered as a unit itself. title: Registry & Retrieval
text: Registry & Retrieval The registry's data model research/questions.yaml holds two top-level collections. A section record has id, num, title, and default_k. A question record has id, section, text, version, k, and status[1]. id is stable once minted: scripts/add_question.py appends a new pending record and prints its id[2], but never mutates an existing record's id, section, or text. A reworded or dropped question gets a new id rather than a rewritten one[3]. version is one of 3.0 / 3.5 / 4.0 / n/a, passed through to ask.py --version[3:1]. It has a default rather than being absent: add_question takes an optional --version X flag and falls back to n/a when omitted[2:1]. The meta corpus's own registry (research/meta/questions.yaml) doesn't use the bucket concept at all. Every question there is n/a[4]. k is the field that's genuinely optional at the per-question level: add_question takes an optional --k N that overrides the section's default_k for that one question only; when a question's k is left null, the answering pipeline reads the section's default_k instead[5]. status starts as pending on append and is later flipped by the answering pipeline to answered if verification passes with no unresolved markers, or needs-review otherwise[5:1]. scripts/recompute_question.py can also flip an existing record's status back to pending while backing up its old answer file, without touching any other record or file[3:2]. Why retrieval differs by corpus For the Spark corpus (the spark profile, scripts/ask.py's default), retrieval is indexed over references/ with multi-qa-mpnet-base-dot-v1, which the architecture doc itself labels "the asymmetric question→passage retriever"[1:1]. That label is contrasted directly with the other corpus this pipeline runs: the meta corpus (this doc's own corpus) uses a different, symmetric embedding model, all-mpnet-base-v2, instead[1:2]. The research rules single out multi-qa-mpnet-base-dot-v1's asymmetric, question-to-passage nature as the reason the retriever's absolute similarity scores run low. Relevance is computed as 2·cos − 1, so rank matters more than the raw number[6]. That's also why the gap-marking gate for Spark-corpus drafting tells writers not to mark a claim [UNRESOURCED] just because a retrieved chunk's relevance score is low or slightly negative: with this asymmetric model, a positive-or-slightly-negative-relevance chunk can still visibly answer the question and should be extracted, and [UNRESOURCED] is reserved for when no retrieved chunk supports any part of the answer at all[6:1]. The two corpora are selected via --corpus {spark,meta} on every pipeline script, and scripts/corpus.py's Corpus dataclass keeps every path and setting for each profile fully separate: registry, per-question answers dir, section-projection dir, content-state sidecar, content manifest, references dir, Chroma path/collection, embedding model, build output, and site title all come from the selected profile rather than a hardcoded constant[1:3]. The Spark corpus is indexed with the asymmetric question→passage retriever multi-qa-mpnet-base-dot-v1, chosen for retrieving over references/, while the meta corpus is indexed with the general symmetric model all-mpnet-base-v2 into its own Chroma collection, meta_docs in .chromadb-meta/[1:4]. That model choice tracks what each corpus actually contains: the meta corpus has no book sources[6:2] and consists of general-purpose prose (docs, rules, agent/skill files describing this repo's own pipeline)[1:5], which is why it uses a symmetric embedding model rather than the Spark corpus's asymmetric one[6:3]. Beyond the embedding model, the two instances share no state at any layer: no registry, no Chroma collection, no content manifest. Each is a fully independent instance of the same pipeline shape (registry question → RAG draft/verify/redraft → section projection → content page → build)[1:6]. The append-only registry research/questions.yaml never has an existing record mutated: new questions are added by appending a fresh pending record, and existing records keep their id, section, and text forever once written[3:3]. Two scripts enforce this: scripts/add_question.py mints a new id and appends a pending record; it never mutates an existing record[3:4][1:7]. scripts/recompute_question.py flips one existing record's status to pending and backs up its old answer file, but touches no other record or file[3:5][1:8]. Separately, scripts/registry.py loads, saves, and validates questions.yaml for the Registry/Section/Question dataclasses[1:9]. The rules also forbid hand-editing an existing record's id, section, or text; a changed question is added as a new record instead of being rewritten in place[3:6]. Because of this, the rest of the pipeline treats questions.yaml as the one-way source of truth: recompute always starts at the registry and flows forward through per-question answers, section projections, and content pages, never the other direction[1:10]. title: Agents & Orchestration
text: Agents & Orchestration Draft, Verify, and Redraft The pipeline splits judgment-requiring work (retrieval, drafting, verifying citations, fixing issues, humanizing prose) into separate agents rather than folding it into deterministic scripts, because that work has no single correct output given its inputs[1]. For the meta corpus these are meta-section-draft, meta-section-verify, and meta-section-redraft, mirrors of the Spark corpus's spark-section-draft/spark-section-verify/spark-section-redraft, adapted to the meta corpus's paths and --corpus meta invocations but not sharing prompt text with them[1:1]. Draft produces one citation-backed answer per question from the local RAG index. It writes the finished answer using an ## <question text> heading with prose beneath, footnotes every factual claim with the source ID ask.py printed, and closes with a ## Sources section[2]. For the meta corpus this same agent role is described as drafting one section of the meta-doc "one citation-backed answer per question," acting as the Draft stage of the meta answering pipeline[3]. Verify checks a drafted section: it validates gaps, checks every cited claim against its underlying chunk, and checks that the ## Sources block is formatted correctly[4]. Redraft is dispatched only if Verify reports issues, and only once, taking those issues as input; after it runs, the section is re-verified a single time. If it still fails after that one redraft-and-re-verify cycle, the answer keeps whatever [NEEDS-REVIEW: ...] markers remain, and the question's registry record is set to needs-review rather than answered[5]. The answer-meta-question skill runs these stages in a fixed sequence for a single question: read the registry record, dispatch Draft, dispatch Verify, dispatch Redraft-if-needed followed by one re-verify, then Humanize, project the section, update the record status, refresh content state, and finally build and commit[5:1]. This order (Draft → Verify → an optional Redraft-then-re-Verify loop → Humanize → downstream projection and build steps → commit) is the same sequence the answering pipeline documents for orchestrating one question end to end[1:2]. Why citations are scoped per question The verify agent's citation check requires two things for every footnoted claim: the source ID must appear on THAT question's own citable source_ids line, and the chunk excerpt under that question must actually support the claim. A footnote whose source ID is not on that question's citable source_ids line is a FAIL even if the underlying fact is true. The claim-support check against that question's own chunk text is the real gate, not the mere existence of the ID somewhere in the corpus[6][4:1]. The reason the same ID can't cross questions is that retrieval is per-question: a source ID retrieved under a different question's block does not license citing it here, because the chunk text returned for that ID differs per question[7]. The Draft stage states the same constraint from the writer's side: answer each question from its own retrieval block only, since a source can be retrieved for several questions but with different chunks, and a fact seen under one question's chunks does not license citing that source under another question unless that question's own chunk text states it. The held-out gate that motivated this rule caught exactly this failure: a true peakExecutionMemory definition retrieved under one question was cited under a different question whose own chunks only held an executor-level table[2:1]. This is why Redraft treats a "misattributed footnote" (source ID not on that question's citable source_ids line) as something to fix rather than wave through: either re-cite to a source ID that is on that question's line and supports the claim, or mark the claim [NEEDS-REVIEW: <reason>] and remove the wrong footnote, never leaving an orphan footnote[8][9]. Humanize and its deterministic backstop The Humanize stage applies prose style to a drafted answer. It is a separate step run by the writing-prose-like-a-human-for-agents:prose-humanizer agent (an installed plugin), not by the Draft/Verify/Redraft agents themselves[10][1:3]. In the per-question skill flow it sits as step 5 of 8, after Draft, Verify, and any Redraft/re-Verify cycle, and before check_prose, project_section, and content_state[1:4][10:1]. For the meta corpus specifically, the humanizer runs against research/meta/answers/q/<id>.md (copied first to a unique scratch path) under hard constraints: it must never touch [^id] footnotes, the ## Sources block, [UNRESOURCED]/[NEEDS-REVIEW] markers, or the ## <question> heading[5:2]. The deterministic backstop is scripts/check_prose.py, described as a "no-LLM lint/backstop" for the Humanize stage[1:5]. It runs in two forms after every humanize pass. Plain check_prose.py <file> lints the humanized file for leftover AI-tell vocabulary (significance inflation, inflated verbs, structural tics such as conclusion phrases or additive transitions, vague attribution), bans curly quotes, and caps em dashes at zero[10:2][1:6]. check_prose.py --diff <before> <after> instead checks that the humanizer didn't touch a protected element: [^id] footnotes, the ## Sources block, [UNRESOURCED]/[NEEDS-REVIEW] markers, the ## <question> heading, or any numeric/config token[10:3][1:7]. For the meta pipeline, both invocations run as uv run python -m scripts.check_prose --diff <scratch-copy> research/meta/answers/q/<id>.md and uv run python -m scripts.check_prose research/meta/answers/q/<id>.md[5:3]. The vocabulary/structural list check_prose applies is a literal blocklist rather than semantic understanding, so it can false-positive on legitimate technical usage (the rule's own example is a Spark phrase about broadcast joins that trips the blocklist even though it is idiomatic)[10:4]. A lint failure is treated as a signal to re-dispatch the humanizer once rather than an automatic hard block[10:5]; in the meta procedure, if either check fails the humanizer is re-dispatched once with the reported issues and both checks re-run, and if still failing the issues are left in place and noted in the final status[5:4]. title: Content, Staleness & Build
text: Content, Staleness & Build Ungenerated vs. stale content_state.py distinguishes the two states by comparing a page's recorded hash in the committed sidecar research/content-state.yaml against the sha256 of the section projection it was assembled from[1]. A page with no entry in that sidecar has never been generated from its section projection, and content_state.py reports it ungenerated[2]. A page has an entry whose recorded hash no longer matches the current projection hash when the section's underlying answers changed since the page was generated or last accepted; content_state.py reports it stale[1:1][2:1]. The required human action differs accordingly. For an ungenerated page, the pipeline generates it: the answer-meta-question skill reads the page's brief: and assembled_from: entries from content/meta/manifest.yaml, writes the page from the projection, humanizes it, then runs content_state --accept <page> to stamp its hash[3]. For a stale page, nothing is overwritten automatically. The pipeline does not edit the page; a human hand-edits it to reflect the changed answers, and only then does content_state.py --accept <page> re-stamp the hash so the page is no longer flagged[2:2][1:2]. This follows from content pages being human-owned once generated: the pipeline never silently overwrites a generated page[4]. Anchors as a frozen cross-repo contract content/manifest.yaml is the single authority for section order, titles, and anchor IDs; content assembly reads anchors from it and never derives them from a Markdown heading or a filename[4:1][5]. Because the anchors are looked up rather than generated from content, other repos can depend on them staying stable, so the project documents them as a frozen cross-repo Integration Contract with the sibling repo sparkforensics[4:2][5:1]. Renaming or removing an anchor is a breaking change, and if the two repos' descriptions of an anchor diverge, the sibling repo's own contract doc wins[4:3]. The contract covers two sets of IDs: the 31 manifest-level anchors, one per content/manifest.yaml entry (enforced by scripts/smoke_content.py's 31-section count check), and 6 sub-anchors nested inside a manifest entry's own page rather than being manifest entries themselves: 4 config-page sub-anchors inside the single config entry (config-shuffle-service, config-autoscale-bounds, config-serializer, config-memory-overhead) and 2 detector-facing sub-anchors, bottleneck-stage-shape and bottleneck-stage-slowness, inside the bottleneck-skew and bottleneck-slow-host entries. All 6 are also enforced by scripts/smoke_content.py[4:4]. The contract applies only to content/manifest.yaml/index.html, i.e. the Spark corpus; content/meta/manifest.yaml and meta.html carry no such contract, so this meta corpus's own anchors may change freely[4:5]. The build's non-fatal staleness warning build.py's HTML-generation role has since been retired: the site build moved from that single Python script (Jinja2 + python-markdown) to a Node pipeline. node site/build-chapters.mjs renders content/manifest.yaml (and content/meta/manifest.yaml) into one committed HTML page per manifest entry, per corpus, under chapters/<spark|meta>/<anchor>.html, via markdown-it and a JS template module (site/templates/chapter-shell.mjs)[1:3][6]. The RAG answering pipeline itself (the registry, per-question answers, section projections, and the staleness model) stayed Python; only HTML generation moved[1:4]. Before rendering, site/build-chapters.mjs shells out to scripts/prebuild_checks.py per corpus (a thin new script, split out of build.py's former inline flow), which calls content_state.report(...), compares each content page's recorded hash (from research/content-state.yaml) against the current section-projection hash, and classifies the page as ungenerated (no recorded entry), stale (hash differs), or up to date (hash matches)[1:5]. If any pages come back ungenerated or stale, it prints the same non-fatal warning banner listing them, but the Node build still produces the output HTML regardless[1:6][2:3]. The warning is non-fatal because content pages are human-owned once generated: the pipeline never overwrites a page's prose automatically, even when its upstream answers have changed[1:7]. A stale or ungenerated flag just means the built page's text may not reflect the latest answers yet. Fixing it requires a human to edit the page (or run first-gen for an ungenerated one) and then re-stamp its hash with content_state.py --accept <page> so it reports up to date again[2:4][1:8]. Recompute itself never triggers first-gen; it only ever flags a page stale, so content pages stay human-owned[1:9].
